title: Why Blood Needs an S-Shaped Carrier

scenes.visual: Title card 'Why Blood Needs an S-Shaped Carrier' over a stream of red blood cells drifting left to right. COLOUR MAP (both films): axes saturation (%) up, PO2 (mmHg) across; adult human curve RED; right-shifted curve ORANGE; one-site carriers TEAL (loose grip dashed, tight grip solid); lung band BLUE at about 100 mmHg; venous-blood band GREY at about 40 mmHg after resting tissue, sliding toward 20 mmHg after hard-working tissue (blood PO2 points, not tissue PO2); release drawn as a vertical GOLD bracket between the lung point and the tissue point; capacity tank RED outline. All curves are computed from the Severinghaus model of standard human blood (P50 26.8 mmHg) or from one-site formulas; every number appears only as on-screen text.

scenes.tts: A litre of plasma carries about three millilitres of oxygen, but a litre of your blood carries about two hundred. What makes up the difference, and how does blood give it up in the right places?
scenes.visual: Two labelled flasks side by side: 'plasma alone' with a thin BLUE layer, label '~3 mL O2 per litre'; 'whole blood' filled deep RED, label '~200 mL O2 per litre'. A question mark hangs between them.
scenes.narration: A litre of plasma carries about three millilitres of oxygen, but a litre of your blood carries about two hundred. What makes up the difference, and how does blood give it up in the right places?

scenes.tts: Plasma is mostly water, and oxygen dissolves poorly in water. The difference rides on hemoglobin, an iron-containing protein packed inside red blood cells.
scenes.visual: Zoom into the RED flask: red cells swim in; one opens to show it packed with small labelled blocks 'hemoglobin', each with four slots. BLUE oxygen dots snap into slots. Label 'iron-containing protein, inside red cells'.
scenes.narration: Plasma is mostly water, and oxygen dissolves poorly in water. The difference rides on hemoglobin, an iron-containing protein packed inside red blood cells.

scenes.tts: Saturation is the share of hemoglobin's binding sites that hold oxygen. Plot it against oxygen pressure, and mark where blood loads and where it unloads.
scenes.caption: Saturation is the share of hemoglobin's binding sites that hold oxygen. Plot it against oxygen pressure (PO2), and mark where blood loads and where it unloads.
scenes.visual: An empty frame draws itself: vertical axis 'saturation (%)' 0 to 100, horizontal axis 'PO2 (mmHg)' 0 to 120. A BLUE vertical band rises at 100, label 'lungs'. A GREY band rises at 40, label 'blood leaving resting tissue'.
scenes.narration: Saturation is the share of hemoglobin's binding sites that hold oxygen. Plot it against oxygen pressure (PO2), and mark where blood loads and where it unloads.

scenes.tts: Blood loads in the lungs, where oxygen pressure is high. At rest, it leaves the tissues at a much lower pressure.
scenes.caption: Blood loads in the lungs, where oxygen pressure is high. At rest, it leaves the tissues at a much lower pressure.
scenes.visual: The BLUE band pulses at 100, label 'lungs: ~100 mmHg'; a red cell icon fills with BLUE dots there. The GREY band pulses at 40, label 'blood leaving resting tissue: ~40 mmHg'; the cell travels across and drops a few dots.
scenes.narration: Blood loads in the lungs, where oxygen pressure is high. At rest, it leaves the tissues at a much lower pressure.

scenes.tts: Each decilitre of blood has a maximum load of oxygen on hemoglobin, its carrying capacity. The load actually carried is capacity times saturation. Hemoglobin releases that capacity times the drop in saturation, from lung to tissue. That drop is the gap between two points on one curve.
scenes.visual: A RED-outlined capacity tank stands left of the frame, label 'capacity (maximum load) ~20 mL O2 per dL (1 dL = 0.1 L)'; beneath it 'carried = capacity x saturation'. On screen: 'oxygen released from hemoglobin = capacity x (saturation in lungs - saturation in tissue)', with a small grey note beneath: '+ a little dissolved O2'. A GOLD bracket sketches between a dot in the BLUE band and a dot in the GREY band, label 'the drop'. Hold the equation a beat before the bracket draws.
scenes.narration: Each decilitre of blood has a maximum load of oxygen on hemoglobin, its carrying capacity. The load actually carried is capacity times saturation. Hemoglobin releases that capacity times the drop in saturation, from lung to tissue. That drop is the gap between two points on one curve.

scenes.tts: Try a simple carrier first, with one binding site per molecule. Give it a loose grip, half full at about the same pressure as blood. In the lungs, it fills only to about four-fifths.
scenes.visual: A TEAL dashed hyperbola (one-site, P50 26.8, computed) draws in. Its dot in the BLUE band sits at '79%', well below the top; a strip of the capacity tank above that level greys out, label 'rides around empty'.
scenes.narration: Try a simple carrier first, with one binding site per molecule. Give it a loose grip, half full at about the same pressure as blood. In the lungs, it fills only to about four-fifths.

scenes.tts: So tighten its grip, until it fills in the lungs. What happens when that blood reaches the tissue?
scenes.visual: A knob labelled 'grip' turns; the TEAL curve slides left and becomes solid (one-site, P50 3, computed). The BLUE-band dot climbs to '97%'. The GREY-band dot is hidden behind a question card.
scenes.narration: So tighten its grip, until it fills in the lungs. What happens when that blood reaches the tissue?

scenes.visual: Predict pause. Question card holds; 5-second ring timer at bottom right.

scenes.tts: It holds on. At tissue pressure it is still nearly full, so it releases almost nothing. Between lung and tissue pressures, a one-site carrier faces a trade-off: fill well, or give up a lot.
scenes.visual: Card lifts: the GREY-band dot sits at '93%'. The GOLD bracket between the two dots is a sliver, label '< 1 mL per dL released'. Two small panels flash: 'loose grip: fills only to ~4/5' and 'tight grip: stays nearly full'. Small label under both: 'between 100 and 40 mmHg'.
scenes.narration: It holds on. At tissue pressure it is still nearly full, so it releases almost nothing. Between lung and tissue pressures, a one-site carrier faces a trade-off: fill well, or give up a lot.

scenes.tts: Hemoglobin escapes the trade-off. Its curve is S-shaped. Near the top it is nearly flat, so a modest fall in lung pressure costs little. Below that, it falls steeply.
scenes.visual: The TEAL curves fade to faint ghosts. The RED S-curve (Severinghaus, computed) draws from left to right: low and flat near zero, rising steeply, then flattening near the top across the BLUE band. Label 'adult human blood'.
scenes.narration: Hemoglobin escapes the trade-off. Its curve is S-shaped. Near the top it is nearly flat, so a modest fall in lung pressure costs little. Below that, it falls steeply.

scenes.tts: At rest, the tissue point sits at the shoulder, where the steep part begins. Blood gives up about a quarter of its oxygen.
scenes.visual: Dots appear on the RED curve: '97.7%' in the BLUE band, '74.9%' in the GREY band at 40, which is tagged 'shoulder'. The GOLD bracket between them fills about a quarter of the capacity tank, label 'about a quarter'.
scenes.narration: At rest, the tissue point sits at the shoulder, where the steep part begins. Blood gives up about a quarter of its oxygen.

scenes.tts: The other three-quarters comes back unused, as a reserve. In hard work, the oxygen pressure of blood leaving active tissue can fall into the steep middle. Now the same blood gives up about two-thirds.
scenes.visual: The GREY band slides left from 40 to 20 (label 'blood leaving hard-working tissue'). The tissue dot rides down the steep RED curve to '32.0%'. The GOLD bracket stretches; the tank drains to about a third full, label 'about two-thirds released'.
scenes.narration: The other three-quarters comes back unused, as a reserve. In hard work, the oxygen pressure of blood leaving active tissue can fall into the steep middle. Now the same blood gives up about two-thirds.

scenes.tts: Why the S? Hemoglobin has four binding sites. In a simple picture, the molecule switches shape as a whole. Each oxygen that binds makes the switch to the high-affinity shape more likely.
scenes.visual: Cartoon: one hemoglobin block with four slots shown in two states, a squarish GREY 'low-affinity shape' and a rounded RED 'high-affinity shape' (schematic two-state picture, no structures; label 'simple picture'). Four still snapshots in a row, with 0, 1, 2 and 3 BLUE dots bound; under each, a bar 'chance of RED shape' that is taller in each snapshot. No animation speed encodes affinity.
scenes.narration: Why the S? Hemoglobin has four binding sites. In a simple picture, the molecule switches shape as a whole. Each oxygen that binds makes the switch to the high-affinity shape more likely.

scenes.tts: So once some sites hold oxygen, the rest fill with a smaller rise in pressure. Emptying runs the same way in reverse. That is cooperative binding.
scenes.visual: Equilibrium snapshots, not a race: a PO2 gauge steps up in equal increments, and beside each step the four-slot block shows how many slots are filled at balance (0, then 1, then 3, then 4). Then the gauge steps down and the slots empty in the same pattern. All transitions at the same steady pace. Beside it the RED S-curve brightens along its steep middle. Label 'cooperative binding'.
scenes.narration: So once some sites hold oxygen, the rest fill with a smaller rise in pressure. Emptying runs the same way in reverse. That is cooperative binding.

scenes.tts: Between these lung and tissue pressures, a one-site carrier cannot both load fully and unload a lot. Cooperative binding lets one carrier load fully in the lungs, and still unload a lot in the tissues.
scenes.visual: Pull back to the full frame: RED curve, BLUE and GREY bands, GOLD bracket at rest and the longer one in hard work, faint TEAL ghosts for comparison.
scenes.narration: Between these lung and tissue pressures, a one-site carrier cannot both load fully and unload a lot. Cooperative binding lets one carrier load fully in the lungs, and still unload a lot in the tissues.

scenes.visual: End card with Hex. Take-home line: 'An S-curve lets one carrier load fully and unload a lot.'
